steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper presenting LOSTU, a fast, non-iterative triangulation method that accounts for camera pose uncertainty. Introduce triangulation, review optimal and practical triangulation methods and their limitations, discuss prior work on camera parameter uncertainty, and state what this paper does.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What triangulation is and where it shows up
- Choosing a method: optimality, scalability, projective invariance; L_{2} vs L_{\infty}
- 2-view, 3-view and multi-view methods; LOST
- Limitations of L_{2} triangulation: geometry, and camera parameter uncertainty
- This paper: LOSTU

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Triangulation is the task of finding the location of a point by intersecting two or more lines-of-position (LOPs). In computer vision applications these LOPs are usually called projection rays, and they come from lines-of-sight (LOS) directions that are transformed from a camera frame into the world frame. This kind of situation comes up naturally in image-based 3D reconstruction and in navigation problems. Practical triangulation algorithms have existed for hundreds of years, but it is still a problem that people study today.

There are several important points to consider when choosing a triangulation method: whether it is optimal, whether it scales to multiple views, and whether it is projective invariant. It can be shown that if we assume Gaussian 2D noise, the solution that minimizes the reprojection error gives the maximum likelihood estimate and is projective invariant. This type of approach is often called L_{2} or optimal triangulation. But this cost function is hard to work with because it has multiple local minima, unlike L_{\infty} triangulation, which has a single local (and so global) minimum.

For 2-view triangulation, the optimal solution can be found by solving for the root of a sixth-order polynomial, and there are faster alternative methods. But the problem quickly becomes intractable when more views are added. For example, for 3 views one has to find the roots of a 47th degree polynomial. There has also been some notable work on speeding up 3-view triangulation, but it does not scale to more points. Triangulation algorithms like the direct linear transform (DLT) and the midpoint method are popular because they scale to multiple views. These methods, or L_{\infty} triangulation, are often used to get an initial estimate, which is then refined iteratively to minimize the reprojection error. The refinement can be slow, though, and it may not converge to the global optimum. Later methods like the linear optimal sine triangulation (LOST) give a closed-form, fast and scalable solution to L_{2} triangulation by weighting the DLT. This framework has been shown to give results that are statistically similar to the common iterative optimal approach.

- Limitations of L_{2}
  - symmetric geometries: all methods similar, no big gain
  - low parallax: L_{2} poor; otherwise substantial improvements over sub-optimal methods
  - optimal only with Gaussian 2D noise + perfect camera parameters
  - midpoint argued for SfM under extrinsic uncertainty, but wrong cost; better to modify L_{2} cost in iterative refinement
  - LOST in spacecraft localization: planetary vs attitude uncertainty, analytical, no numerical simulation
- This paper
  - camera pose uncertainty; intersection/resection equivalence: "planetary position uncertainties" -> "camera center uncertainties"
  - LOSTU: general, uncertainty-aware, non-iterative
  - simulations; maximum likelihood sequential reconstruction pipeline

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Triangulation is the task of finding the location of a point by intersecting two or more lines-of-position (LOPs). In computer vision applications these LOPs are usually called projection rays, and they come from lines-of-sight (LOS) directions that are transformed from a camera frame into the world frame. This kind of situation comes up naturally in image-based 3D reconstruction and in navigation problems. Practical triangulation algorithms have existed for hundreds of years, but it is still a problem that people study today.

There are several important points to consider when choosing a triangulation method: whether it is optimal, whether it scales to multiple views, and whether it is projective invariant. It can be shown that if we assume Gaussian 2D noise, the solution that minimizes the reprojection error gives the maximum likelihood estimate and is projective invariant. This type of approach is often called L_{2} or optimal triangulation. But this cost function is hard to work with because it has multiple local minima, unlike L_{\infty} triangulation, which has a single local (and so global) minimum.

For 2-view triangulation, the optimal solution can be found by solving for the root of a sixth-order polynomial, and there are faster alternative methods. But the problem quickly becomes intractable when more views are added. For example, for 3 views one has to find the roots of a 47th degree polynomial. There has also been some notable work on speeding up 3-view triangulation, but it does not scale to more points. Triangulation algorithms like the direct linear transform (DLT) and the midpoint method are popular because they scale to multiple views. These methods, or L_{\infty} triangulation, are often used to get an initial estimate, which is then refined iteratively to minimize the reprojection error. The refinement can be slow, though, and it may not converge to the global optimum. Later methods like the linear optimal sine triangulation (LOST) give a closed-form, fast and scalable solution to L_{2} triangulation by weighting the DLT. This framework has been shown to give results that are statistically similar to the common iterative optimal approach.

It is important to understand the limitations of L_{2} triangulation. First, there are some geometries (typically symmetric ones) where all triangulation methods perform about the same, so optimal triangulation does not give a big performance gain there. Also, low-parallax geometries are a typical case where L_{2} triangulation does poorly. Still, in general scenarios that are not symmetric and do not have low parallax, L_{2} triangulation can give substantial improvements over sub-optimal methods.

Second, minimizing the reprojection error is only optimal if we assume Gaussian 2D noise on the image measurements and perfect knowledge of the camera parameters. Prior work argues that the midpoint method should be used instead of L_{2} optimal triangulation in the SfM process because of uncertainties in the extrinsic camera parameters. But the midpoint method still inherently minimizes the wrong cost function. A more appropriate approach when the camera parameters are uncertain is to modify the L_{2} cost function in the iterative refinement process, as other work has done. Motivated by the challenges in spacecraft localization, the LOST algorithm has been used to analyze analytically how important planetary uncertainty is relative to spacecraft camera attitude uncertainties. The equations there again have the form of a linear system, but that work did not do any numerical simulation to validate the method, since it concluded that these effects were mostly negligible in spaceflight.

In this paper we study triangulation under camera pose uncertainty carefully and look at the effects on performance for traditional triangulation methods. Using the geometric equivalence between intersection and resection, we show that “planetary position uncertainties” become “camera center uncertainties” in a reconstruction scenario. We extend the earlier framework and introduce LOSTU, a general uncertainty-aware and non-iterative framework for triangulation. Existing studies, such as the study arguing for the midpoint method and a study using iterative refinement, either do not have uncertainty-aware optimal triangulation methods or use iterative refinement inside a larger framework. So we run simulations to validate LOSTU experimentally and to show the advantages of taking camera parameter uncertainties into account. We also show these benefits in a maximum likelihood sequential reconstruction pipeline.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Triangulation describes the task of localizing a point by the intersection of two or more lines-of-position (LOPs). In computer vision applications, these LOPs are usually referred to as projection rays and originate from lines-of-sight (LOS) directions that are transformed from a camera frame into the world frame. Such situations arise naturally in image-based 3D reconstruction and navigation problems. Although practical triangulation algorithms have existed for hundreds of years [1], triangulation remains a problem of contemporary study.

Several important points must be considered when choosing a triangulation method: its optimality, its scalability to multiple views, and its projective invariance. It can be shown that, under the assumption of Gaussian 2D noise, the solution minimizing the reprojection error provides the maximum likelihood estimate and is projective invariant [2]. This type of approach is often called L_{2} or optimal triangulation, but its cost function is difficult to work with because it has multiple local minima [3], unlike L_{\infty} triangulation [4,5], which has a single local (and thus global) minimum.

In 2-view triangulation, the optimal solution can be found by solving for the root of a sixth-order polynomial [3], and faster alternative methods exist [6,7]. Yet the problem quickly becomes intractable as more views are added; for example, 3 views require finding the roots of a 47th degree polynomial [8]. Some notable work has also been done to speed up 3-view triangulation [9,10], but it does not scale to more points. Triangulation algorithms like the direct linear transform (DLT) [2] and the midpoint method [3] are popular due to their scalability to multiple views. These, or L_{\infty} triangulation [11], are often used to obtain an initial estimate that is then iteratively refined to minimize the reprojection error. However, the refinement can be slow and may not converge to the global optimum. Subsequent methods, like the linear optimal sine triangulation (LOST), yield a closed-form, fast, and scalable solution to L_{2} triangulation by weighting the DLT [1]. This framework has been shown to give statistically similar results to the common iterative optimal approach [12].

Understanding the limitations of L_{2} triangulation is essential. First, there are certain geometries (typically symmetric ones) under which all triangulation methods perform similarly [3,1], so that optimal triangulation does not offer substantial performance gains. Furthermore, low-parallax geometries are a typical example where L_{2} triangulation performs poorly [3,13]. Nevertheless, L_{2} triangulation can provide substantial improvements over sub-optimal methods in general scenarios that are not symmetric and do not have low parallax [3,1].

Second, minimizing the reprojection error is only optimal under the assumptions of Gaussian 2D noise on the image measurements and perfect knowledge of the camera parameters. Reference [14] argues that the midpoint method should be used over L_{2} optimal triangulation in the SfM process because of uncertainties in the extrinsic camera parameters. However, the midpoint method still inherently minimizes the wrong cost function. A more appropriate approach under camera parameter uncertainties is to modify the L_{2} cost function in the iterative refinement process, as is done in Ref. [15,16,17]. Spurred by challenges in spacecraft localization, the LOST algorithm has been used to analytically assess the relative importance of planetary uncertainty and spacecraft camera attitude uncertainties [18]. While the equations again feature a linear system, no numerical simulation validating that method was done in Ref. [18], since it concluded that these effects were mostly negligible in spaceflight.

This paper carefully studies triangulation under camera pose uncertainty and addresses its performance effects on traditional triangulation methods. Using the geometric equivalence between intersection and resection [1], we show that “planetary position uncertainties” become “camera center uncertainties” in a reconstruction scenario. We extend the framework in Refs. [1,18] to introduce LOSTU: a general uncertainty-aware and non-iterative framework for triangulation. Existing studies, like Ref. [14] and [16], either lack uncertainty-aware optimal triangulation methods or use iterative refinement within a larger framework. We therefore perform simulations to experimentally validate LOSTU and the advantages of considering camera parameter uncertainties, and further demonstrate these benefits in a maximum likelihood sequential reconstruction pipeline.
